papers.title: Prospects of Detecting Cosmological Domain Walls in the Cosmic Microwave Background
papers.authors: Berkin Gürbüz, Robert Brandenberger, Yitian Sun
papers.abstract: Topological defects are a generic prediction of field theories with spontaneously broken symmetries, and domain walls, the two-dimensional defects left by a broken discrete symmetry, are among the simplest. We study the imprint of dark, purely gravitationally interacting domain walls on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), in the regime where a low symmetry-breaking scale $\eta$ allows the walls to evade the Zel'dovich overclosure bound while remaining cosmologically relevant. The relativistic repulsion of matter by a planar wall carves out an evacuated void bounded by an overdense shell, and we compute the resulting photon deflection field analytically for walls both aligned with and arbitrarily inclined to the line of sight. The deflection stamps coherent, strongly non-Gaussian distortions onto the temperature sky, with a characteristic two-peak structure set by the relativistic displacement scale and an inclination dependence that vanishes for face-on walls. Because these signatures are localised and anisotropic, they are poorly captured by two-point statistics; we therefore analyse them with a curvelet/wavelet decomposition matched to the wall's geometry, and with simulation-based inference, training a Neural Posterior Estimator (NPE) to recover the scattering redshift $z$, energy scale $\eta$, and inclination $\theta$, and a Neural Ratio Estimator (NRE) to evaluate the likelihood-ratio test statistic for limit-setting. Casting these methods as sensitivity forecasts for a South Pole Telescope-like (SPT) survey, we find that the curvelet and wavelet statistical thresholds populate a common $\eta \sim 10-100$ MeV band over the accessible redshift range. The neural-ratio sensitivity curve, which exploits the full map morphology, reaches a factor 1.3-1.9 lower in $\eta$ at $z \gtrsim 20$, or $\sim 2-7$ in the wall tension, landing essentially on the per-resolution-element noise floor.

conclusions: A planar domain wall's repulsive gravity creates a caustic-free, evacuated void of half-width $\psi(z)$ bounded by an overdense matter shell inside the causal horizon; this imprints an antisymmetric, two-peaked photon deflection field onto the CMB that vanishes completely when the wall is viewed face-on ($\theta = \pi/2$).

For an idealized SPT-like survey, directional curvelet and wavelet kurtosis statistics can detect domain walls with symmetry-breaking scales in the band $\eta \sim 10\text{--}100\,\mathrm{MeV}$ across the accessible redshift range.

Simulation-based inference via a Neural Ratio Estimator (NRE) exploits the full 2D map morphology to improve sensitivity by a factor of $1.3\text{--}1.9$ in $\eta$ at $z \gtrsim 20$ (corresponding to a factor of $\sim 2\text{--}7$ in wall tension $\sigma \propto \eta^3$), reaching the instrumental per-pixel noise floor.

A Neural Posterior Estimator (NPE) trained on single CMB patches accurately recovers the wall's inclination angle $\theta$ independently, while revealing a geometric degeneracy between the scattering redshift $z$ and energy scale $\eta$.

ai.summary: Domain walls are sheet-like topological defects that form in the early universe when a discrete symmetry is spontaneously broken, separating patches of space that settled into different vacuum states. While high-energy walls would quickly dominate the cosmic energy budget (the Zel'dovich overclosure bound), walls formed at lower symmetry-breaking energy scales ($\eta \lesssim 100\,\mathrm{MeV}$) remain cosmologically viable and exert a repulsive gravitational force perpendicular to their surface. In this paper, the authors analytically compute how a planar domain wall repels surrounding matter after matter-radiation equality—carving out an evacuated void bordered by a compressed, overdense shell—and derive the resulting gravitational lensing deflection of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) photons. Because this lensing stamps localized, line-like, non-Gaussian distortions onto the CMB temperature map that standard two-point power spectra miss, they forecast detectability for a South Pole Telescope-like (SPT) survey using directional wavelets (curvelets) and neural simulation-based inference (SBI), showing that neural likelihood-ratio estimators can push sensitivity right down to the instrumental noise floor.

papers.title: AMICO galaxy clusters in KiDS-1000: Cosmological constraints from the two-point correlation function
papers.authors: Massimiliano Romanello, Giorgio Francesco Lesci, Federico Marulli, Lauro Moscardini, Carlo Giocoli, Matteo Maturi, Mario Radovich, Sandro Bardelli, Gianluca Castignani, Hendrik Hildebrandt, Lorenzo Ingoglia, Shahab Joudaki, Emanuella Puddu, Mauro Sereno
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the clustering properties of an optically identified photometric galaxy cluster catalogue from KiDS-1000. The sample was identified by the AMICO algorithm and consists of 9049 clusters with $S/N\geq3.5$, in the redshift range $0.1\leq z<0.8$, spread over an effective area of 838.78 deg$^2$. Clusters are selected according to their observed intrinsic richness, with thresholds of $\lambda^*{obs}\geq 20,25,30$ within $0.10\leq z<0.30$, $0.30\leq z<0.45$ and $0.45\leq z<0.80$, respectively. We measure the multipoles of the two-point correlation function over different ranges of scales from 5 $h^{-1}$ Mpc to 150 $h^{-1}$ Mpc. We model the clustering signal in the context of the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, accounting for the main observational effects, such RSDs and photo-$z$ uncertainties. The effective bias of the cluster sample is estimated via a mass-richness scaling relation. For the MCMC analysis, we adopt Gaussian priors on the parameters of the mass-richness scaling relation, and broad, uniform priors to derive cosmological constraints on the cold matter density parameter, the power spectrum amplitude and the structure growth parameter, $S_8\equiv\sigma_8 \sqrt{\Omega{m}/0.3}$. Specifically, we find $\Omega_{m}=0.24^{+0.02}{-0.02}$ and $\sigma_8=0.86^{+0.13}{-0.10}$ representing an improvement in precision over both the 2D and 3D AMICO clustering analyses performed on the previous KiDS data release. Moreover, we obtain $S_8=0.77^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ in $1\sigma$ agreement with the AMICO KiDS-1000 number counts constraints estimated from the same catalogue, as well as with some results from external early- and late-Universe data sets. Our work strengthens the potential of cluster clustering as a complementary and competitive probe, to be included and further developed with the final KiDS-Legacy data release, and in other future Stage-IV photometric redshift surveys.

conclusions: The analysis constrains the total matter density to $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.24 \pm 0.02$ and the matter fluctuation amplitude to $\sigma_8 = 0.86^{+0.13}_{-0.10}$, improving the figure of merit by a factor of $1.8$ over previous KiDS-DR3 cluster clustering studies.

The low inferred matter density ($\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} = 0.24$) agrees with the cluster abundance results from the same KiDS-1000 catalogue, though it stands in a mild $\sim 2\sigma$ tension with Planck 2018 CMB measurements ($\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} \approx 0.315$).

The derived structure growth parameter $S_8 \equiv \sigma_8 \sqrt{\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3} = 0.77^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ is consistent within $1\sigma$ with both cosmic shear analyses (KiDS-1000, KiDS-Legacy) and Planck CMB constraints, due to the relatively large uncertainty on $\sigma_8$.

Photometric redshift uncertainties ($\sigma_z = 0.014(1+z)$) and the algorithm's redshift discretisation ($\Delta z = 0.01$) dominate the small-scale damping of the clustering monopole and artificially boost the quadrupole and hexadecapole, whereas virial Finger-of-God velocity dispersions are subdominant for clusters.

ai.summary: Galaxy clusters trace the highest density peaks of the cosmic web, making their spatial clustering a powerful probe of large-scale structure growth that is less affected by non-linearities and small-scale virial motions ('Fingers of God') than ordinary galaxies. A key advantage of clusters over standard galaxy clustering is that their mass can be estimated via observable proxies—such as 'intrinsic richness' ($\lambda^*$), roughly the membership-weighted count of bright cluster galaxies—which allows one to compute the cluster bias theoretically from the halo mass function and break the classic degeneracy between bias and the fluctuation amplitude $\sigma_8$. In this paper, the authors measure the 3D two-point correlation function multipoles (monopole, quadrupole, and hexadecapole) of 9,049 optically selected clusters across $0.1 \le z < 0.8$ from the Kilo Degree Survey (KiDS-1000), identified using the AMICO optimal-filtering algorithm (one of the two cluster finders adopted by Euclid). By modelling linear redshift-space distortions, Alcock–Paczynski geometric distortions, and line-of-sight damping from photometric redshift errors alongside a weak-lensing-calibrated mass–richness relation, they obtain independent late-time $\Lambda$CDM constraints on $\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $S_8$, testing consistency with cluster number counts and cosmic shear ahead of Euclid and LSST.

papers.title: Cluster connectivity in DES Y3 data: impact on galaxy properties
papers.authors: C. Gouin, C. Laigle, J. Prat, L. O.V. Edwards, P. Ganeshaiah Veena, D. Galárraga-Espinosa, G. Gopidas
papers.abstract: Connectivity, namely the number of cosmic filaments reaching out of groups or clusters, has recently emerged as an informative way to quantify environment. With the advent of wide-area photometric surveys, it becomes possible to measure connectivity on a statistically significant sample of clusters. In this work, we extract the cosmic web from the DES Y3 photometric data and measure the connectivity around clusters from several public catalogs up to $z < 1$. Cosmic filaments are extracted in 2D with DisPerSE (the parametrization of which is calibrated on simulations) in tomographic slices of fixed comoving thickness of 220 Mpc, with a constant sampling across the redshift range ($\sim 0.1$ galaxies Mpc$^{-2}$). We first recover the well-established trend that cluster connectivity increases with cluster mass at all redshifts. We then investigate the properties of cluster member galaxies and find that, at fixed mass, clusters with a higher fraction of red (elliptical) galaxies are more strongly connected to the cosmic web. Furthermore, by examining the radial profiles of the red and elliptical galaxy fractions, we obtain hints that galaxy populations may undergo pre-processing within filamentary structures before being accreted into clusters. Overall, we demonstrate that despite photometric redshift uncertainties and projection effects, our method allows for the quantification of the cosmic web environment around clusters in broad-band photometric surveys. This work is consistent with results based on the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1). We plan to publicly release the cluster connectivity catalog as well as the cosmic filament catalog.

conclusions: Cluster connectivity correlates positively with cluster mass ($M_{500c}$) across all redshift bins up to $z < 0.9$, showing good consistency with recent Euclid Q1 measurements and no significant redshift evolution.

At fixed cluster mass, more connected clusters host a significantly higher fraction of evolved galaxies, showing partial Pearson correlations of $\rho \approx 0.17\text{--}0.23$ ($p \le 4.6 \times 10^{-6}$) for the red galaxy fraction at $0.2 < z < 0.6$ and $\rho \approx 0.21\text{--}0.22$ ($p \le 2.1 \times 10^{-9}$) for the elliptical galaxy fraction at $0.2 < z < 0.4$.

Galaxies located within $0.1\,\text{Mpc}$ of cosmic filament spines around clusters (out to $4 R_{500c}$) exhibit a higher fraction of red and elliptical members than the isotropic average at the same cluster-centric radius; the excess is stronger for colour than morphology, indicating that filament-driven pre-processing quenches star formation faster than it transforms spiral galaxies into ellipticals.
ai.relevance_reason: Provides loose background on cosmic web filament extraction in wide-field photometric surveys (including comparisons to Euclid Q1), though the focus is on observational galaxy evolution and quenching rather than non-linear cosmological modelling, beyond-ΛCDM simulations, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: In the cosmic web, galaxy clusters sit at the nodes where large-scale matter filaments intersect, and a cluster's "connectivity"—the number of filaments feeding into it—characterizes its large-scale accretion environment and merger history. Because photometric surveys have large line-of-sight distance uncertainties that blur 3D structure, the authors reconstruct the cosmic web in 2D tomographic slices of comoving thickness $\sim 222\,\text{Mpc}$ across $\sim 4130\,\text{deg}^2$ of Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) data up to $z \sim 0.9$. Using the topological filament-finding algorithm DisPerSE across 50 Monte Carlo realizations of the galaxy photometric redshifts, they measure the connectivity within $2 R_{500c}$ for X-ray (eRASS1, RASS) and Sunyaev–Zel'dovich (ACT, SPT) selected clusters and cross-correlate it with the colours and neural-network-classified morphologies of member galaxies. This demonstrates that wide-field broadband imaging surveys like DES and Euclid can reliably map the cosmic web and probe "pre-processing"—the quenching of star formation and morphological transformation of galaxies inside filaments before they even fall into a cluster.

papers.title: Semi-Analytic Predictions for Strong-Lensing Perturbers in Cold and Self-Interacting Dark Matter
papers.authors: Jonathan Tekverk, Duncan K. Adams, Simon Birrer, Rouven Essig, Daniel Gilman
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing is sensitive to the abundance and internal structure of dark matter halos, providing a probe of gravothermal evolution in self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). We combine semi-analytic cold dark matter (CDM) subhalo histories with a model for gravothermal evolution in SIDM to generate CDM and SIDM subhalo populations across SIDM parameter space. We predict their projected enclosed masses and deflection-based projected density slopes and compare them with three perturbers inferred through gravitational imaging in PJ011646, SDSS J0946+1006, and JVAS B1938+666. For SIDM model parameters $\sigma_0/m_\chi=147.1$ cm$^2$/g and $w=120$ km/s, SIDM subhalos reproduce all three perturbers more often than CDM subhalos. For PJ011646, we find ~0.6 cored SIDM subhalos per host matching the perturber, compared with ~0.002 in CDM, while core-collapsed subhalos are too steep. For SDSS J0946+1006, we find ~3 core-collapsed and ~0.004 cored SIDM subhalos per host, compared with none in 900 CDM realizations, although baryons, neglected here, may matter for such massive subhalos. For "detection V" in JVAS B1938+666, we find ~220 core-collapsed and ~20 cored SIDM subhalos per host within the $2\sigma$ posterior region, compared with ~0.2 in CDM; the CDM candidates require exceptionally early accretion, at median redshift $z\sim13$. Simultaneously reproducing all three perturbers requires $w\gtrsim10^2$ km/s, so that the massive (~$5.6\times10^{10}M_\odot$) progenitors of SDSS J0946+1006 candidates can collapse, and is achieved for $\sigma_0/m_\chi\gtrsim10^2$ cm$^2$/g in the parameter sets studied. Our results show how semi-analytic models can quantify how often subhalos reproduce individual perturbers in different dark matter models, and our modular framework can be readily updated as models of tidal stripping and late-stage gravothermal evolution in SIDM improve. (abridged)

conclusions: Under a fiducial velocity-dependent SIDM model ($\sigma_0/m_\chi = 147.1\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$, $w = 120\text{ km/s}$), SIDM subhalos match all three observed strong-lensing perturbers significantly more often than CDM counterparts across $10^{13}\,M_\odot$ host halo realizations.

For the massive, dense perturber in SDSS J0946+1006 (evaluated at $R_{\text{pivot}} \simeq 0.63\text{ kpc}$), zero matching subhalos are found across 900 CDM realizations, whereas SIDM produces $\sim 3$ core-collapsed candidates per host halo.

For the low-mass "detection $\mathcal{V}$" perturber in JVAS B1938+666 ($R_{\text{pivot}} \simeq 90\text{ pc}$), SIDM yields $\sim 220$ core-collapsed and $\sim 20$ cored subhalos per host within the $2\sigma$ observational region compared to $\sim 0.2$ in CDM, with the rare CDM candidates requiring extreme early infall ($z_{\text{infall}} \sim 13$, in the earliest $0.1\%$ of accretion histories).

For the intermediate-slope perturber in PJ011646 ($R_{\text{pivot}} \simeq 1.92\text{ kpc}$), core-collapsed halos are too steep, but cored SIDM subhalos still match the perturber $\sim 300$ times more frequently than CDM ($\sim 0.6$ vs. $\sim 0.002$ per host).

Simultaneously explaining all three perturbers within a single velocity-dependent SIDM model requires a cross-section normalization $\sigma_0/m_\chi \gtrsim 10^2\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$ and a turnover velocity $w \gtrsim 10^2\text{ km/s}$ so that the massive ($\sim 5.6 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$) progenitors of the SDSS J0946+1006 candidates can undergo core collapse.

ai.summary: Strong gravitational lensing—where a foreground galaxy bends light from a background source into extended arcs or multiple images—allows cosmologists to detect otherwise invisible, starless dark matter "subhalos" via localized distortions in the lensed images ("gravitational imaging"). Several recently detected lensing perturbers appear surprisingly compact and steep compared to standard cold dark matter (CDM) expectations, motivating explanations using self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), in which particle collisions transport heat inside halos and drive a "gravothermal" evolution from an initial flat core to a hyper-dense "core-collapsed" state. Because high-resolution $N$-body simulations of core collapse are computationally prohibitive across many host halos and parameter choices, the authors combine the semi-analytic subhalo merger-tree code `SatGen` with a calibrated parametric model of SIDM gravothermal and tidal evolution to rapidly generate thousands of subhalo populations. They compute the 2D projected enclosed masses and density slopes of these synthetic subhalos and compare them directly against three well-known strong-lensing perturbers (in PJ011646, SDSS J0946+1006, and JVAS B1938+666). This modular, fast framework enables statistical scans over SIDM cross-section parameters to test whether a single dark matter model can naturally explain the diverse internal structures of observed lensing perturbers.

papers.title: The Impact of Inclination, Redshift, and Mass Ratio Selection on Cosmological Constraints from Bright Sirens Beyond Conventional Fisher Approximations
papers.authors: Gustavo B. F. Lima, Rafael F. Aranha, Rodrigo S. Gonçalves
papers.abstract: Future generations of gravitational-wave observatories are projected to detect up to thousands bright siren events within a decade of operation. However, the precision of these cosmological forecasts depends heavily on the astrophysical assumptions embedded within the simulation pipelines. In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of variations in the binary mass ratio ($q$), the maximum observable inclination angle ($\iota_{\max}$), and the maximum redshift ($z_{\max}$) on the constraints of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$). We perform our analyses based on the GWDALI framework, the GW Doublet Approximation, and the phenomenological waveform approximant IMRPhenomD. By adopting sets of non-spinning binary neutron star populations we explore the impact of astrophysical parameters on the constraints of cosmological parameters. Our results reveal a clear dichotomy in the observational requirements: while the statistical uncertainty on $H_0$ falls below the falls below approximately $1.3\%$ level for $N \ge 400$ events and drops under $0.9\%$ once $N \ge 800$, a deep-redshift catalog ($z_{\max} \ge 1.0$) is strictly required to effectively break parameter degeneracies and constrain the global geometry through $\Omega_m$. Furthermore, expanding the maximum inclination cutoff from the conservative $20^{\circ}$ up to $40^{\circ}$ substantially mitigates the correlation between distance and inclination.

conclusions: Statistical uncertainty on $H_0$ reaches $\lesssim 1.3\%$ with $N \ge 400$ bright siren events and drops below $0.9\%$ for $N \ge 800$ events, confirming that $H_0$ precision is driven primarily by total sample size and local distance calibration.

Breaking parameter degeneracies to tightly constrain the matter density $\Omega_m$ strictly requires a deep-redshift catalog ($z_{\max} \ge 1.0$) to probe the cosmic expansion history beyond the local linear Hubble flow.

Relaxing the maximum observable jet inclination cutoff from a conservative $20^{\circ}$ to $40^{\circ}$ (motivated by off-axis structured gamma-ray burst models) substantially mitigates the correlation between luminosity distance and orbital inclination.

Variations in the binary mass ratio ($q$) distribution introduce subtle shifts in the simulated signal-to-noise ratio distribution that alter the likelihood geometry, meaning waveform and population assumptions will become dominant systematics for sub-percent third-generation GW cosmology.

ai.summary: "Bright sirens" are gravitational-wave (GW) mergers—typically binary neutron stars—accompanied by an electromagnetic counterpart (like a short gamma-ray burst) that provides the host galaxy's redshift, allowing us to pair redshift with the GW-inferred luminosity distance to measure cosmic expansion. A major hurdle in standard siren cosmology is that the GW strain amplitude depends on both distance and the binary's orbital inclination angle ($\iota$), creating a strong distance–inclination degeneracy where standard Gaussian Fisher matrix approximations often fail. In this paper, the authors use the GWDALI framework (which incorporates higher-order derivative expansions beyond the Fisher approximation to capture non-Gaussian posteriors) alongside IMRPhenomD phenomenological waveforms to simulate non-spinning binary neutron star populations for third-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer. They systematically vary astrophysical selection assumptions—specifically the binary mass ratio ($q$), the maximum inclination angle ($\iota_{\max}$) at which an electromagnetic jet remains detectable, and the redshift depth ($z_{\max}$)—to quantify how population modelling choices propagate into flat-$\Lambda$CDM constraints on $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$.

papers.title: Introducing the GION Lightcone Simulation Suite for Multi-Wavelength Large-Scale Structure Cosmology
papers.authors: Ken Osato, Satoshi Tanaka, Tomoaki Ishiyama, Hironao Miyatake, Takahiro Nishimichi, Masato Shirasaki
papers.abstract: We present the GION (Ginkaku Lightcone Multi-wavelength Simulation Project) simulation suite: 10 full-sky high-resolution cosmological lightcone simulations and their associated products for multi-wavelength large-scale structure cosmology. We use the TreePM $N$-body code GINKAKU, which is highly optimized in the massively parallel environment, and integrate the on-the-fly lightcone construction technique. Each lightcone simulation is run with $6144^3$ particles in a volume of $(1.5 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{Gpc})^3$, which corresponds to a particle mass of $1.28 \times 10^9 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$, and extends to $z = 5$. The fine mass resolution and the depth of the lightcone simulations allow us to resolve dark matter halos down to $10^{11} \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$ in the high-redshift Universe, which is crucial for applications to the Stage-IV cosmological surveys. The fundamental statistics of the simulations, including the matter power spectrum, halo power spectrum, and halo mass function, are validated against theoretical predictions. We also generate various large-scale structure observables from the lightcone outputs: the dark matter halo catalogs, mock galaxy samples, weak lensing convergence maps, and thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) maps. The angular power spectra of these observables, including the cross-correlation between weak lensing and the tSZ effect, are in good agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating that the suite provides mutually consistent multi-wavelength observables on the same lightcone. The GION simulation suite will be publicly available and can be used for various cosmological analyses to address the observational systematic effects and validate theoretical models.

conclusions: The suite provides 10 statistically independent full-sky lightcone realizations out to $z=5$ (each ~10.1 TB of public data), resolving halos down to $6.38 \times 10^{10} \, h^{-1}\mathrm{M}_\odot$ (50 particles) with $25 \, h^{-1}\mathrm{Mpc}$ radial shells on $N_{\mathrm{side}}=8192$ HEALPix grids ($0.429\text{ arcmin}$ pixel size).

Fixed-redshift matter power spectra agree with the `DarkEmulator2` neural-network emulator within a few percent for $k \gtrsim 0.1 \, h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ across $0 \le z \le 4$, and halo mass functions match theoretical expectations within $5\%$ for $10^{11} \lesssim M_{\mathrm{200b}}/h^{-1}\mathrm{M}_\odot \lesssim 10^{13}$.

Weak lensing convergence ($\kappa$) angular power spectra match theoretical predictions within a few percent across $30 \lesssim \ell \lesssim 5000$, while mock galaxy clustering, tSZ, and kSZ auto- and cross-spectra agree with halo-model/perturbative predictions within $\sim 10\%$ on large/intermediate scales before showing expected non-linear excesses of $15\text{--}50\%$ at $\ell \gtrsim 10^3$.

Because the simulations are dark-matter-only in a fixed Planck 2018 $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, baryonic effects and gas pressure profiles are pasted in post-processing (neglecting baryonic backreaction), and weak lensing is computed under the Born approximation (ignoring lens-lens coupling and post-Born ray-tracing effects).
ai.relevance_reason: While this is a major $N$-body lightcone simulation suite for Stage-IV surveys with convergence testing and emulator validation, it is strictly limited to a single fixed Planck $\Lambda$CDM cosmology using standard TreePM and the Born approximation, rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM models, approximate solvers, or relativistic ray-tracing.
ai.summary: Modern "Stage-IV" galaxy surveys (like Euclid, DESI, and LSST) and cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments observe the same underlying cosmic web at different wavelengths, including secondary CMB distortions like the thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) effects—where CMB photons scatter off hot, high-pressure cluster gas or bulk-moving ionized gas, respectively. Cross-correlating these probes with galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing breaks parameter degeneracies, but testing joint analysis pipelines requires simulations with both huge volumes and fine enough mass resolution to capture the relatively small halos ($M \sim 10^{11} \, h^{-1}\mathrm{M}_\odot$) that host high-redshift emission-line galaxies (ELGs). The authors present the GION suite: 10 independent, full-sky $\Lambda$CDM $N$-body simulations evolved with the massively parallel TreePM code `GINKAKU` on the Fugaku supercomputer ($6144^3$ particles in a $1.5 \, h^{-1}\mathrm{Gpc}$ box, initialized at $z=24$ with 3LPT via `monofonIC`). Rather than stacking discrete redshift snapshots, GION outputs particles continuously on-the-fly as they cross the backward lightcone out to $z=5$, immediately processing them into `MPI-Rockstar` halo catalogs and high-resolution HEALPix density and momentum shells before deleting the raw particle data to save storage. From these shared lightcones, they generate and validate mutually consistent mock galaxy catalogs, weak lensing convergence maps, and baryon-pasted tSZ/kSZ maps that are publicly released as a testbed for multi-wavelength survey pipelines.

papers.title: Luminosity-weighted galaxy and gravitational wave cross-correlations
papers.authors: Charles Dalang, Isabela Santiago de Matos, João Ferri, Raul Abramo, Tessa Baker
papers.abstract: Cross-correlations of galaxies and gravitational waves (GW) can be used to extract cosmological parameters and the gravitational wave bias. In this work, we study how to include galaxy luminosities in these spatial cross-correlations, inspired by the standard approach of dark sirens line-of-sight redshift priors. We present a formalism to include luminosity information in galaxy-GW simulations and study the effects of assigning a hosting probability that depends on luminosity through a simple power law $p_{\rm{host}} \propto L^\beta$ with $\beta \in \{0,1,2\}$ corresponding to uniformly, linear and quadratically weighted in luminosity. This effectively changes the GW linear bias with respect to dark matter and, in principle, allows to gain signal-to-noise and a sharper measurement of cosmological parameters. For a realistic luminosity dependence of the galaxy bias taken from DESI data, the gain is marginal, making the method robust to different luminosity weighting prescriptions. We show that the cross-correlation inference is able to recover the injected GW bias within $10\%$ if there is a mismatch between the injected linear bias of host galaxies and observed galaxies, provided that one sticks to relatively large scales. We also show that the Hubble constant and matter energy density can be recovered to $0.5\%$ and $5\%$ respectively with a third generation network of GW detectors, regardless of the modeling of the GW bias.

conclusions: Using realistic luminosity-dependent galaxy biases derived from DESI DR1 data, weighting galaxies by $p_{\rm host} \propto L^\beta$ ($\beta \in \{0, 1, 2\}$) produces only marginal improvements in cosmological constraints because the linear bias gradient across luminosity bins is relatively shallow.

If GW mergers occur in an unobserved galaxy population whose linear bias differs from that of the observed galaxy survey, the true GW linear bias $b_{\rm gw}$ can still be recovered within $\sim 10\%$ precision (with $2\%$ on $H_0$ and $26\%$ on $\Omega_{\rm m}$), provided the analysis is restricted to linear angular scales ($\ell_{\rm max} = 110$).

Pushing to smaller angular scales ($\ell_{\rm max} = 190$) introduces systematic biases in the inferred $b_{\rm gw}$ due to non-linear clustering, but the background cosmological parameters remain unbiased and tighten significantly to $0.5\%$ for $H_0$ and $5\%$ for $\Omega_{\rm m}$ for a 5-year ET+2CE forecast.

Unlike standard line-of-sight dark siren pipelines—which can suffer systematic biases if the host galaxy luminosity weighting is mismodelled—spatial galaxy-GW cross-correlations ("Peak Sirens") are highly robust against uncertainties in how GW mergers populate galaxies of different luminosities.
ai.relevance_reason: While the paper touches on luminosity-dependent galaxy bias and $H_0$ constraints, it focuses on gravitational wave dark siren cross-correlations rather than non-linear LSS theory, beyond-ΛCDM simulations, or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Gravitational wave (GW) "dark sirens"—binary mergers without an electromagnetic counterpart—provide direct luminosity distances $D_L$ but lack redshifts, so cosmologists cross-correlate their sky maps with spectroscopic galaxy surveys (in redshift $z$) to constrain the $D_L(z)$ expansion history and the clustering bias of GW hosts ($b_{\rm gw}$). Because more luminous galaxies are typically more massive and more strongly clustered, it is common to weight potential host galaxies by their luminosity ($p_{\rm host} \propto L^\beta$), which increases the effective galaxy bias and should theoretically boost the cross-correlation signal-to-noise ratio. In this paper, the authors incorporate luminosity-dependent galaxy clustering calibrated on the DESI DR1 Bright Galaxy Survey into the "Peak Sirens" tomographic angular cross-correlation pipeline (`GLASS` light-cone simulations paired with `NaMaster` pseudo-$C_\ell$ estimators). Forecasting 5 years of observations with third-generation GW detectors (Einstein Telescope + two Cosmic Explorers, ~70,000 binary black hole events) cross-correlated with a DESI DR3-like survey, they evaluate how luminosity weighting ($\beta = 0, 1, 2$) and mismatches between the true GW host population and observed galaxies affect parameter recovery. This work demonstrates that spatial cross-correlation methods are remarkably immune to astrophysical uncertainties in how GW binaries populate galaxies, avoiding a major systematic vulnerability of traditional line-of-sight dark siren analyses.

papers.title: Joint Angular-Power Distributions of Interfering Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
papers.authors: Yan-Chen Bi, Yu-Mei Wu, Qing-Guo Huang
papers.abstract: Finite populations of supermassive black-hole binaries produce fluctuations in both gravitational-wave power and pulsar timing correlations. We characterize the realization-dependent, orientation-averaged Earth-term angular correlation through its frequency-resolved Legendre coefficients. A hybrid model of bright sources and a Gaussian faint background extends the conditional Gamma distribution in the many-weak-source limit to non-central $\chi^2$ statistics, yielding correlated multipoles after population marginalization. Our analytical variance decomposition and SMBHB population simulations reveal a population-dependent transition from interference dominated variance at low frequencies to population-power-dominated variance at high frequencies. In the many-weak-source regime, a multivariate lognormal approximation captures the main features of the joint distribution using only the first two log-cumulants. These results provide statistical benchmarks for fluctuations in both the overall amplitude and angular structure of the realized correlation.

Decomposing the variance of the quadrupole $S_2$ across SMBHB population simulations reveals a frequency-dependent crossover: wave interference between many faint binaries dominates the realization-to-realization scatter at low frequencies ($f \sim 2\,\mathrm{nHz}$), whereas Poisson shot noise in total source power from rare, bright binaries dominates at high frequencies ($f \sim 30\,\mathrm{nHz}$).

Marginalizing over total GW power fluctuations couples different angular multipoles $\ell$ and $\ell'$; in the low-frequency, many-weak-source regime, their joint distribution is accurately captured by an analytic multivariate lognormal approximation using only the first two log-cumulants ($\mu_\ell$ and covariance $\Sigma_{\ell\ell'} = \mathrm{Var}[\ln h] + \delta_{\ell\ell'}\psi_1(n_\ell)$).

papers.title: Modelling kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space using hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion
papers.authors: Eishica Chand, Arka Banerjee
papers.abstract: Higher-order statistics are becoming increasingly useful in clustering studies of the large-scale structure (LSS) of the universe. The kNN-CDFs are one such higher-order statistic, sensitive to all N-point correlations and easy to compute on data. Utilising their statistical gains for cosmological inference requires modelling them accurately for the tracer of interest. We use the hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion to enable this modelling in redshift space, building and validating the pipeline on Quijote simulations. We show that the kNN-CDFs of a luminous red galaxy (LRG)-like sample can be modelled down to scales as small as r = 10 Mpc/h, with the minimum reliable scale increasing with nearest-neighbour order. Moreover, the model parameters inferred from the kNN-CDFs also describe the galaxy power spectrum P(k), indicating model consistency across the two statistics and the feasibility of combining them. Fisher forecasts for galaxy auto clustering show that combining P(k) and kNN-CDFs improves constraints on all parameters relative to either statistic alone. Relative to P(k), the constraints on $b_3$ improve the most, while those on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ improve by factors of 3.5 and 1.7, respectively. Including galaxy-matter cross clustering alongside galaxy auto clustering further improves the Fisher constraints from both P(k) and kNN-CDFs, with their combination yielding the tightest constraints overall. Relative to P(k), the largest improvement from this combination is found for $b_2$, while the constraints on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ improve by factors of 4.2 and 1.7, respectively. These results demonstrate the applicability of the hybrid Lagrangian bias framework to model the kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space, and the potential of combining higher-order and two-point statistics to extract cosmological information.

conclusions: The hybrid Lagrangian bias + RSD model accurately predicts redshift-space $k$NN-CDFs (and joint galaxy–matter $k$NN-CDFs) down to $r = 10\,\mathrm{Mpc}/h$ for $1$NN, with the minimum reliable scale shifting to larger $r$ for higher $k$ because higher-order neighbours probe denser, more non-linear regions.

Bias and RSD parameters fit purely to the $k$NN-CDFs simultaneously provide an accurate prediction of the galaxy power spectrum $P(k)$ in both real and redshift space (whereas best-fit parameters from $P(k)$ alone fail to reproduce the $k$NN-CDFs due to parameter degeneracies).

In Fisher forecasts for redshift-space galaxy auto-clustering, combining $P(k)$ and $k$NN-CDFs breaks bias degeneracies—especially for the cubic bias $b_3$—and tightens constraints on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ by factors of $3.5$ and $1.7$ compared to $P(k)$ alone.

Adding galaxy–matter cross-clustering via joint $k$NN-CDFs alongside auto-clustering yields even tighter combined constraints, improving $\sigma_8$ by a factor of $4.2$ and $\Omega_m$ by $1.7$ (with the largest bias improvement on $b_2$) relative to $P(k)$.

papers.title: Non-Markovian Cosmology with Causal Memory Kernels
papers.authors: Aritra Sanyal, Prabir Rudra
papers.abstract: We investigate a non-Markovian extension of Friedmann cosmology in which the present expansion rate retains information about the past cosmic evolution through a causal memory kernel, with \LCDM{} recovered in the limit of vanishing kernel amplitude, $A\to0$. We show that five kernels (Linear, Power Law, Exponential, Gaussian and Oscillatory) arise as cosine transforms of the spectral densities of an unresolved hidden sector, and that the Exponential and Linear kernels also follow independently from Israel-Stewart causal viscosity and from Deser-Woodard non-local gravity, respectively. We constrain the kernels with 30 Cosmic Chronometer (CC) measurements and with $H(z)$ derived from the DESI DR1 and DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, using multi-start $\chi^{2}$ minimisation followed by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and compare them with \LCDM{} through the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. The Linear amplitude is consistent with zero ($A=0.002\pm0.030$ for CC+DR2). The Power-law, Exponential and Gaussian kernels are observationally degenerate: the data select sharply peaked kernels that constrain only an integrated amplitude $\Aeff\simeq0.01$--$0.03$, equivalent to a uniform $0.5$--$1.5\%$ rescaling of $H(z)$, and they are disfavoured relative to \LCDM{} ($\Delta{\rm AIC}=+2.5$ to $+3.6$). Only the Oscillatory kernel improves the fit appreciably ($\dchi=4.5$--$8.1$), but it requires a negative damping rate, which is incompatible with the causal derivations, and it is not favoured once CC data are included ($\Delta{\rm BIC}=+4.4$ to $+6.2$)

conclusions: All five memory kernels can be derived microscopically via the Zwanzig–Mori projection formalism by coupling the Ricci scalar to a bath of hidden oscillators, while the Exponential and Linear kernels also follow independently from Israel–Stewart causal bulk viscosity and the short-lag limit of Deser–Woodard non-local gravity, respectively.

The Linear memory kernel is completely consistent with standard $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$, with its dimensionless amplitude tightly bounded around zero ($A = 0.002 \pm 0.030$ for CC + DESI DR2), limiting universal leading-order memory effects to $|A| \lesssim 0.06$ at $2\sigma$.

The Power-law, Exponential, and Gaussian kernels are observationally degenerate in the short-memory limit ($\alpha, \beta \gtrsim 50$, $\sigma \ll 1$), where they act as a Dirac delta function that merely rescales $H(z)$ by $0.5\text{--}1.5\%$ ($A_{\rm eff} \simeq 0.01\text{--}0.03$, equivalent to shifting $H_0$ by $\lesssim 1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$) and are disfavoured by information criteria ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = +2.5$ to $+3.6$).

The Oscillatory kernel achieves the largest fit improvement ($\Delta\chi^2 = 4.5\text{--}8.1$, preferring a redshift-lag period $\Delta z \simeq 1.2\text{--}1.5$), but requires an unphysical negative damping rate ($\alpha < 0$, meaning memory grows into the past) and is disfavoured once Cosmic Chronometer data are added ($\Delta\mathrm{BIC} = +4.4$ to $+6.2$).

However, coarse-graining over small-scale inhomogeneities, integrating out unresolved hidden-sector fields, or including non-local gravitational and dissipative fluid effects can naturally introduce a "memory" of past expansion into the Friedmann equation. The authors formulate a non-Markovian extension of $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ by adding a causal memory integral over past redshifts, demonstrating that five mathematical memory kernels (Linear, Power-law, Exponential, Gaussian, and Oscillatory) correspond to specific microscopic models such as open-system environmental spectral densities, Israel–Stewart bulk viscosity, and Deser–Woodard non-local gravity. They test these kernels against 30 Cosmic Chronometer (CC) $H(z)$ measurements and radial BAO data from DESI DR1 and DR2 (holding baseline $\Lambda\mathrm{CDM}$ parameters fixed to Planck 2018 values) using MCMC sampling to see if late-time expansion data favour cosmic memory.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks vs U-Net: Application to thermal dust emission recovery in the microwave
papers.authors: Nicolas Morant Juan, José M. Casas, Laura Bonavera
papers.abstract: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

conclusions: Both the PINN and U-Net achieve strong morphological and spectral reconstruction of the 353 GHz dust map across all tested PySM dust models (D4, D7, D10) and Galactic latitudes, maintaining a Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) $> 0.96$ and matching the true angular power spectrum slope ($\alpha_d$ in $C_\ell \propto \ell^{-\alpha_d}$) to within $1\%$.

The unconstrained U-Net achieves slightly lower pixel-wise root-mean-square error (RMSE of $1.75 \times 10^{-4}\,K_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ vs. $2.01 \times 10^{-4}\,K_{\mathrm{CMB}}$ on the validation set) because its output is not restricted to a three-parameter physical bottleneck.

Enforcing hard thermodynamic bounds ($A > 0$, $\beta \in (1, 3)$, $T \in (10, 40)\,\mathrm{K}$) via the MBB output layer guarantees physically admissible predictions without degrading spatial structure or power spectrum fidelity ($300 \le \ell \le 2000$).

Because the networks were only trained against a single target frequency (353 GHz), the intermediate $A$, $\beta$, and $T$ maps are degenerate; extending the loss to enforce multi-frequency consistency is needed to break parameter degeneracies and solve the full inverse problem.

papers.title: Finite-distance effects and scalar suppression in massive gravity
papers.authors: Chris Choi, Tina Kahniashvili, Barnabás Póczos
papers.abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) probe the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background through the angular cross-correlations of timing residuals. For a GW background in general relativity (GR), the expected overlap reduction function (ORF) is given by the Hellings--Downs (HD) correlation. We investigate how a nonzero graviton mass modifies this prediction through a massive dispersion relation and additional vector and scalar polarizations, producing a modified effective ORF. In the massive limit, the finite-distance pulsar terms survive angular averaging, multiplying the correlations of all three polarization sectors by a pulsar-dependent factor that can enhance, suppress, or reverse them. We adopt a tensor Earth--Earth normalization that preserves the continuous finite-distance effect. In the massless limit, we find that the vector ORF vanishes and the scalar ORF approaches a finite breathing mode. We propose the phenomenological prescription $\Omega_S/\Omega_T=A_S(m_g/\omega)^{n_S}$, with scalar amplitude parameter $A_S$ and suppression index $n_S>0$. These results provide a consistent framework for future PTA analyses of massive gravity.

conclusions: In the massive limit ($v_g \to 0$), the finite-distance pulsar terms do not average away over the sky, multiplying the correlations of tensor, vector, and scalar modes by a pulsar-dependent phase factor that can enhance, suppress, or reverse the signal.

Normalizing the ORF by twice the tensor Earth–Earth response ($2\Gamma^{00,\text{GR}} = 4\pi/3$) smoothly interpolates between the autocorrelation and infinite-distance cross-correlation limits, shifting the coaligned correlation for nearly equidistant real pulsar pairs (like J2124$-$3358 and J1744$-$1134) to $\simeq 0.82$ instead of the standard $1/2$.
As $m_g \to 0$, the vector ORF naturally vanishes as $(m_g/\omega)^2$, whereas the scalar ORF approaches a finite breathing-mode correlation rather than zero.

Introducing the phenomenological scalar suppression $\Omega_S/\Omega_T = A_S(m_g/\omega)^{n_S}$ with $A_S \geq 0$ and $n_S > 0$ mimics Vainshtein-like decoupling and ensures uniform recovery of the standard GR tensor correlation in the massless limit.

If the graviton has a nonzero mass ($m_g \neq 0$), gravitational waves travel slower than light and gain three extra polarization states (two vector and one scalar) in addition to the two standard tensor modes, altering this angular correlation pattern. The authors analytically derive the full effective ORF in massive gravity while retaining finite-distance "pulsar terms"—contributions from the gravitational wave acting at the pulsars' locations that are usually dropped under the assumption that pulsars are infinitely far away, but which remain coherent for slow-moving massive gravitons or pulsar pairs at similar distances. papers.title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-ray Weakness
papers.authors: Shi-Jiang Chen, Jun-Xian Wang, Zhen-Ya Zheng, Ruqiu Lin, Luis C. Ho, Zhen-Yi Cai, Chang-Hao Chen, Zsofi Igo, Jia-Lai Kang, Ruancun Li, Teng Liu, Wenke Ren, Zhen-Bo Su
papers.abstract: A major question about JWST's little red dots (LRDs) at $z\sim4-8$ is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broad-band limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At $z\sim0.3$, similarly luminous sources require $\sim10^{3-4}$ less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: "X-normal" LLRDs resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas the "X-weak" stack lies $\sim0.5-0.7$ dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at $\sim3.3\sigma$ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame $\sim2-3$ keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona ($\Delta\alpha_{\mathrm{ox}}\sim-0.1$ to $-0.2$) with Compton-thin absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}}\sim10^{22-23}$ cm$^{-2}$), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

conclusions: The six local analogs split into two distinct populations: two "X-normal" galaxies that match standard unobscured quasar X-ray relations and show optical variability, and four "X-weak" galaxies that lack optical variability, have redder continua, and closely mirror high-$z$ LRDs.

Stacking three of the X-weak local analogs yields a $\sim 3.3\sigma$ detection in the rest-frame $2-8\text{ keV}$ band (dominated by $2-3\text{ keV}$ photons), placing their X-ray luminosity $\sim 0.5-0.7\text{ dex}$ below standard unobscured AGN scaling relations—a constraint tighter than $95\%$ of individual high-$z$ LRD limits achieved with $\sim 1000\times$ less exposure time ($\sim 40\text{ ks}$ vs. $\sim 40\text{ Ms}$).

The relatively hard spectral shape of the X-weak stack (detected at $2-3\text{ keV}$ with a $3\sigma$ upper limit on the $0.5-2\text{ keV}$ soft band) rules out simple unobscured super-Eddington models ($\Gamma \sim 3.4$), which underpredict the $2-3\text{ keV}$ flux by $\sim 0.6-1.5\text{ dex}$ or violate the soft-band limit.

The X-ray constraints and strong optical Balmer decrements ($\mathrm{H}\alpha/\mathrm{H}\beta \gtrsim 7-8$) are best and most simply explained by a mildly intrinsically X-ray-weak corona ($\Delta\alpha_{\mathrm{ox}} \sim -0.1$ to $-0.2$) viewed through moderate, Compton-thin gas absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}} \sim 10^{22-23}\text{ cm}^{-2}$), rather than extreme Compton-thick ($N_{\mathrm{H}} \gtrsim 10^{24.5}\text{ cm}^{-2}$) obscuration.

At high redshift, even megasecond X-ray exposures cannot easily distinguish whether this X-ray deficit is caused by extreme "Compton-thick" gas obscuration, intrinsically weak X-ray coronae, or rapid "super-Eddington" accretion (where matter falls onto the black hole faster than the standard radiation-pressure limit, steepening the X-ray spectrum so fewer high-energy photons reach us). To bypass this observational bottleneck, the authors use the Einstein Probe Follow-up X-ray Telescope (EP-FXT) to observe six "local little red dots" (LLRDs) at $z \sim 0.3$—compact "green pea" dwarf galaxies whose V-shaped UV-to-optical spectra and broad emission lines closely mimic high-$z$ LRDs, but whose proximity requires $\sim 10^{3}-10^{4}$ times less exposure time and provides direct access to diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. papers.title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
papers.authors: Yoann L. Launay
papers.abstract: The theory of Inflation, supplemented by fluctuations of the quantum vacuum, is the leading paradigm to explain the correlations of inhomogeneities at very large distances in the Universe. Particle physics methods fail when strong non-linearity and non-perturbativity are involved, leaving a whole landscape of untestable scenarios of inflation. Starobinsky's stochastic inflation can in principle treat inflationary inhomogeneities nonlinearly and classically as the Hubble radius becomes smaller than their wavelengths, but it was never formulated in full general relativity, which motivates this thesis. Using the Keldysh formalism of nonequilibrium quantum field theory, we first develop a validity criterion for the use of classical computations, and thus simulations, to probe inflationary interactions, finding analytically that the bispectrum can be extracted from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetimes. We then provide the first analytical solutions to the constraints for inhomogeneous initial conditions of numerical relativity simulations of inflation, and use them to explore its nonperturbative regime. Our main contribution is to obtain stochastic equations for the full set of inflaton equations in general relativity: this description incorporates the full nonlinear and backreacting evolution, is small-gauge-invariant, and is free of historical assumptions such as the gradient-free separate universe approximation. We implement these equations in the BSSN formulation of numerical relativity, demonstrating their correctness in slow-roll and ultra slow-roll scenarios via the satisfaction of the constraints, with a first look at eternal inflation. Finally, we extend our coarse-graining methods beyond General Relativity and single-field inflation, offering a phenomenological framework with the ambition of serving as a numerical particle collider for the early universe.

conclusions: Using the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism of non-equilibrium quantum field theory, the author establishes a quantitative criterion for when classical field simulations accurately capture inflationary self-interactions, showing that three-point correlations (the bispectrum) can be reliably extracted starting from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetime.

The thesis derives the first analytical solutions to the ADM Hamiltonian and momentum constraint equations for strongly inhomogeneous scalar-field initial conditions in numerical relativity, enabling exact simulations of the non-perturbative inflationary regime.

A complete set of covariant, small-gauge-invariant stochastic equations for the inflaton and metric in full GR is derived and implemented in 3+1 BSSN numerical relativity, successfully preserving the relativistic constraints across slow-roll, ultra-slow-roll, and eternal inflation regimes without assuming spatial gradients vanish on super-Hubble scales.

The coarse-graining framework is extended beyond single-field GR to accommodate multiple fields and modified gravity theories in the early universe, providing a general numerical toolkit for probing strongly non-linear primordial physics.

Standard perturbation theory breaks down when these fluctuations become strongly non-linear—such as in scenarios producing primordial black holes or eternal inflation—and existing non-perturbative approaches like "stochastic inflation" rely on the "separate universe" approximation, which treats different Hubble patches as evolving independently and ignores spatial gradients and full general relativistic (GR) effects. In this PhD thesis, the author formulates stochastic inflation in full 3+1 numerical relativity (using the BSSN formalism) by splitting fields into long-wavelength classical backgrounds and short-wavelength quantum noise sources that continuously cross the horizon. By combining non-equilibrium quantum field theory with exact solutions to the GR constraint equations, this framework allows numerical relativity simulations to self-consistently track non-linear inflationary dynamics and gravitational backreaction without relying on the separate-universe approximation.

papers.title: Gauge-field energy density in inflationary kinetic-coupling models: QFT regularization versus horizon cutoffs
papers.authors: A.O. Naidenko, O.O. Sobol, S.I. Vilchinskii
papers.abstract: Coupling gauge fields to the inflaton can amplify their quantum fluctuations during inflation, with potential applications to a range of cosmological phenomena. A central challenge is to define finite and physically meaningful observables, such as the gauge-field energy density. In this work, we study an Abelian gauge field kinetically coupled to the inflaton through $f^2(\phi)F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ in a de Sitter background with $f\propto a^{\gamma_1}$, and compare conventional quantum-field-theoretic regularization with horizon-cutoff prescriptions. Using a hard physical-momentum cutoff and dimensional regularization, we derive the ultraviolet divergences in closed form and fix the remaining one-parameter finite-part ambiguity by requiring the coupling-induced total energy density to be nonnegative. We then examine five horizon-cutoff prescriptions based on characteristic scales of the mode equations. Their predictions depend sensitively on the choice of horizon scale and, for weak gauge-field production, can deviate substantially from the regularized result; for the adopted finite-part prescription, the minimal horizon agrees best with the regularized total energy density. As $|\gamma_1|\to 2$, where infrared modes dominate, the relative deviation of all prescriptions from the regularized result vanishes, independently of the finite-part prescription. Outside this regime, the separate electric and magnetic contributions, which can become negative after regularization, are not reliably reproduced by any of the horizon-cutoff prescriptions.

conclusions: Using hard physical-momentum cutoff and dimensional regularization, the authors derive closed-form analytical expressions for the quartic, quadratic, and logarithmic UV divergences of the gauge-field energy density, fixing the remaining one-parameter finite ambiguity by requiring the total coupling-induced energy density to be non-negative and electric–magnetic symmetric ($\gamma_1 \to -\gamma_1$).

In the weak-production regime ($|\gamma_1|$ not near $2$), standard horizon-cutoff prescriptions deviate substantially from the QFT-regularized energy density, depend strongly on the exact choice of horizon scale, and often violate electric–magnetic duality symmetry or fail to vanish where the coupling-induced contribution should be zero ($\gamma_1 = \pm 1$).

Among the five tested horizon cutoffs, the "minimal horizon" prescription agrees best with the total QFT-regularized energy density across the parameter range $(-2 < \gamma_1 < 2)$, while all five prescriptions converge to the exact regularized result as $|\gamma_1| \to 2$, where amplified infrared modes dominate over UV vacuum fluctuations.

Away from the infrared-dominated limit ($|\gamma_1| \to 2$), none of the horizon-cutoff prescriptions reliably reproduce the separate electric ($\rho_E$) and magnetic ($\rho_B$) energy densities—which can become individually negative after QFT regularization—meaning that backreaction terms on the inflaton ($\propto \rho_E - \rho_B$) are highly sensitive to the regularization scheme.
